first.rationale: The two live symptoms are onboarding completion (-4%) and activation (-6%), which is exactly the causal chain memory_86 (shorter onboarding -> completion + time-to-value) and memory_31 (fewer signup fields -> durable first-week activation lift) speak to. Fixing the funnel is the more sustainable lever than matching the competitor's price: memory_73 explicitly warns that promotional pricing bought acquisition at the cost of 30-day retention, which directly conflicts with the sustainable-qualified-revenue objective, so I am deliberately not chasing the price war even though it is the loudest event. memory_57 (referral) and memory_44 (enterprise sales-assist) are both credible but address segments that are not currently degrading, so they do not use the single slot well; memory_91 (activation messaging) is the strongest runner-up and stays queued if onboarding verification comes back weak. I am spending both verification pulls on memory_86 and memory_31 because they are the load-bearing evidence for my choice and because they may be partially redundant observations of the same effect - if they are, my confidence in a combined signup+onboarding simplification is inflated, and memory_31 is 64 days old (day 12), so its 'durable' lift may predate the current product and traffic mix. Downstream value risk is real and flagged: cutting signup fields and onboarding steps can raise raw activation while degrading lead qualification data and routing, which would show up as more activated accounts but less *qualified* revenue - so the experiment must be instrumented on downstream qualified pipeline and 30/60-day retention, not just completion and activation rates. Running at standard experiment scale rather than broad rollout precisely because the inherited evidence is aging and possibly double-counted; if the archived records show the two memories are one effect or came from a materially different funnel, I will drop to a small guarded test or pivot to activation_messaging.

mid.rationale: Verification came back clean and, importantly, showed the two memories are NOT redundant: exp_86 is a post-signup onboarding flow change (completion +13%, time-to-value -2.1d, 30-day retention +3%) while exp_31 is a signup-field change (signup +15%, activation +9%, retention -1%, qualified revenue +4%, SMB only). So the combined confidence I held going in was not inflated by double-counting, and I proceed with simplify_onboarding at standard experiment scale. The weight shifts toward the exp_86 half of the intervention: it is the only inherited result that improves completion, time-to-value AND 30-day retention simultaneously, which is the cleanest match to the sustainable-qualified-revenue objective and directly addresses both live symptoms (completion -4%, activation -6%). The exp_31 half I scope narrowly to SMB and treat as the weaker leg: its record explicitly says it did not replicate on other segments, and it carries a -1% retention drag, so cutting signup fields is not something I extend company-wide off this evidence. I continue to decline promotional_pricing despite the competitor's entry pricing, because memory_73 remains the direct counter-evidence - acquisition and revenue lift purchased with materially worse 30-day retention is the wrong trade against a long-term objective, and matching a price war is the loudest option rather than the best one. referral_incentive and enterprise_sales_assist stay unused this cycle: both are credible but target segments that are not currently degrading. activation_messaging (memory_91) remains the queued fallback. Residual uncertainty I am holding rather than resolving: exp_31 is 64 days old and SMB-scoped so its 'durable' lift may not survive the current traffic mix; and the downstream value risk stands - fewer signup fields and fewer onboarding steps can inflate raw activation while thinning lead-qualification data and routing quality, producing more activated accounts and less qualified revenue. Success criteria are therefore downstream qualified pipeline and 30/60-day retention, not completion and activation rates alone; if qualified revenue per activated account degrades, I roll back the signup-field leg first and keep the onboarding-flow leg.

final2.rationale: Holding the decision. The competitor's second cut and the doubling of churn conversations are a change in pressure, not a change in evidence, and I should not let urgency substitute for a reason to reverse. Nothing arrived this week that weakens exp_86 (completion +13%, time-to-value -2.1d, 30-day retention +3%) or that strengthens the case for discounting. If anything, the case for promotional_pricing is weaker than it looks: memory_73 records it as an ACQUISITION lever for price-sensitive SMB, with materially worse 30-day retention. It is not evidence that discounting retains accounts already in churn conversations. Using it here would be borrowing support from a result about a different problem, and buying short-lived accounts with a known retention penalty is close to the opposite of maximizing sustainable long-term qualified revenue. There is also a strategic trap in matching a price war against an entrant who has just demonstrated willingness to cut twice: we would be committing our one slot to a move the competitor can undercut again next week, while our own funnel decay goes unaddressed. The two live symptoms remain completion -4% and activation -6%, and simplify_onboarding is the only direction with verified evidence of improving both plus 30-day retention. I keep the scope from my last decision: the onboarding-flow leg (exp_86) carries the weight; the signup-field leg (exp_31) stays SMB-scoped and is the first thing rolled back, since it is 64 days old, unreplicated outside SMB, and carries a -1% retention drag. Downstream value risk still flagged: leaner signup and onboarding can lift raw activation while thinning lead-qualification data and routing, inflating activated accounts and deflating qualified revenue. Judge on downstream qualified pipeline and 30/60-day retention, not completion and activation alone. Uncertainty I am explicitly not pretending away: I have no verified evidence about what actually retains price-sensitive SMB under competitive pressure, and this experiment does not answer that. The right response to the churn wave this week is non-experimental - direct retention outreach, save offers handled case by case by the account team, and instrumenting why these accounts are leaving - none of which consumes the single experiment slot. I would spend next cycle's verification budget on memory_73's source record and on whatever churn data we gather, so that if we do price-respond later it is on evidence rather than on the loudest event of the morning.
